24 vacant seats, a new delimitation plan: Centre's Bill puts PoJK back in focus
articles.summary: Srinagar: A proposed delimitation Bill has made a specific provision for redrawing Jammu and Kashmir Assembly constituencies in the territory under Pakistan’s occupation if the occupation ends, while leaving unanswered questions about the 24 seats reserved for the area under the existing constitutional framework. Section 3(4) of the Delimitation (Second) Bill, 2026, provides that the Election Commission of India will act as the Delimitation Commission for Assembly constituencies falling in the territory once it ceases to be under occupation. The provision is conditional and does not envisage any immediate delimitation. The Bill is scheduled to be introduced in the Lok Sabha on November 30. The 24 Assembly seats have a history predating the 2019 reorganisation of the erstwhile state. Section 48 of the former state of Jammu and Kashmir Constitution provided that these seats would remain vacant until the territory ceased to be under Pakistan’s occupation and its residents elected representatives. YSRCP to support delimitation Bill if it provides for a 50% increase in seats Originally 25, their number was reduced to 24 through a constitutional amendment in 1975. The arrangement was carried forward under Section 14(4) of the J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019. The seats are not counted while calculating the membership of the present elected Assembly. J&K currently has 90 elected Assembly constituencies, 43 in Jammu and 47 in Kashmir. The 24 reserved seats are additional to these. However, the proposed Bill does not expressly mention these 24 seats or clarify how its provision would operate alongside the existing arrangement. It also does not specify whether the proposed 50 per cent increase in legislative seats would apply to them. Another notable feature is that the Election Commission itself has been assigned the delimitation responsibility for the occupied territory. For other areas, the Bill provides for a separate Delimitation Commission headed by a sitting or retired Supreme Court judge, with the Chief Election Commissioner or an Election Commissioner and the State Election Commissioner as members. The proposal comes amid renewed political debate over the 2022 delimitation exercise in J&K, which increased the number of elected Assembly constituencies from 83 to 90. Jammu received six additional seats, taking its tally to 43, while Kashmir received one, taking its tally to 47. The distribution was questioned by several Valley-based political parties, which argued that it did not adequately reflect the population difference between the two regions. PDP president and former chief minister Mehbooba Mufti on Saturday invoked that experience while criticising the Centre’s fresh delimitation proposals. In a post on X, she said J&K had repeatedly been used as a testing ground for political experiments and that parties elsewhere in the country should learn from its experience. Her remarks came as southern states, including Karnataka, raised concerns over the implications of the proposed nationwide delimitation exercise for their political representation. The proposed legislation is yet to be considered by Parliament.

articles.summary: Mysuru: Former Puducherry Lieutenant Governor and IPS officer Kiran Bedi urged the government to introduce a dedicated care leave provision for parents of children with disabilities , which enables them to balance professional commitments with the special care and attention their children require. “Just as maternity and paternity leave are provided, the government should consider introducing care leave for parents of children with special abilities,” she said. She was speaking after inaugurating the two-day 32nd National Parents’ Meet, organised by PARIVAAR, the National Confederation of Parent Organisations, in association with Maulana Azad National Urdu University, Hyderabad, and the All India Institute of Speech and Hearing (AIISH), at the AIISH premises in Mysuru on Saturday. India's maternity rights framework needs a paternity leave rethink The meet is hosted with the theme of ‘From Care to Empowerment: Building Inclusive Communities Through Strong Families and Collective Action’. She said that families must become active participants in shaping policies and securing the rights of persons with disabilities. Suggesting the formation of separate awareness, advocacy and activism groups, she called for mobilising parents, professionals, lawyers and corporate leaders to identify gaps in policy implementation and pursue collective action. Bedi also stressed the need for measurable outcomes from such initiatives, urging families to move beyond discussions and demonstrate concrete progress. She called for greater involvement of fathers in caregiving, observing that the responsibility of raising children with disabilities should not fall entirely on mothers. Advocating a change in societal attitudes, she said persons with disabilities must be treated with dignity and provided opportunities for independence, empowerment and inclusion. She called upon the trust to immediately address the issue, strengthen the trust’s corpus and ensure that it fulfilled its intended purpose of supporting children beyond their parents’ lifetime. PARIVAAR President Dr Pankaj Maru said that the organisation represented more than 300 parent and non-parent organisations across the country. AIISH Director Dr Pushpavathi highlighted the institute’s contributions for rehabilitation and early intervention for such kids. NIEPID Director BV Ramkumar emphasised the importance of family-centred rehabilitation of such kids. Dr D K Menon and B Elangovan, Deputy Director, Technical Education, JSS, were present.

articles.title: Why link women's quota to delimitation exercise, asks Javed Akhtar; questions govt intent
articles.summary: Pune: Renowned scriptwriter and lyricist Javed Akhtar on Saturday questioned the linking of women's reservation to the delimitation exercise, saying the two issues should be dealt with separately. It is like placing women and children in front during a war so that nobody fires, while delimitation is brought in from behind, he opined. Akhtar was speaking to reporters after receiving the Mahatma Phule Samata Award 2026 at a ceremony organised by the Akhil Bharatiya Mahatma Phule Samata Parishad to mark the death anniversary of social reformer Mahatma Jyotiba Phule. "Why have you included it (women's quota) in this (delimitation)? It is like placing women and children in front during a war so that nobody fires, while delimitation is brought in from behind. If the intention is right, separate the women's reservation part from it. That bill had already been passed," he said. Union Cabinet clears fresh delimitation-linked women quota bill Major opposition parties had expressed their willingness to pass a separate bill on women's quota. Akhtar pointed out. The final details of the delimitation exercise, including the formation of new constituencies and the criteria behind it, were yet to be made public, Akhtar added. It appears areas that did not follow family planning are being given more seats, he said, adding it would be important to see which opposition leaders backed the move. The Constitution (132nd Amendment) Bill, 2026, seeks to raise the Lok Sabha's maximum strength to 850, with up to 815 members from states and 35 from Union territories. It also raises the ceiling for a state assembly from 500 to 650. The BJP on Saturday said the Delimitation Bill is not just a legislative reform but a decisive commitment to inclusive democracy and women's rightful place in nation-building, asserting that the moment has arrived to fulfil the commitment to India's 'Nari Shakti'. The ruling party said the proposed framework will increase Lok Sabha seats by 50 per cent across states, ensuring broader parliamentary representation, and also pave the way for 33 per cent reservation for women in the 2029 Lok Sabha elections.

articles.title: ‘Last bus to save democracy’: I.N.D.I.A. bloc to try to convince DMK and NCP(SP) to oppose Delimitation Bill
articles.summary: New Delhi: The I.N.D.I.A bloc is projecting the fight against Modi government’s delimitation plans as the “last bus to save democracy” and will try to convince DMK and NCP(SP) that its passage will open the road for the BJP to ensure two-third Parliamentary majority in perpetuity, sources said. With Lok Sabha all set to take up the Constitution (132nd Amendment) Bill, 2026 on Monday, the Opposition leaders decided to “highlight” how representation of Dalits and tribals will be negatively impacted as their latest population figures are not considered as also the presence of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s presence in the Delimitation Commission. At a meeting of floor leaders chaired by Congress president and Leader of Opposition in Rajya Sabha Mallikarjun Kharge, sources said leaders were of the view that the smooth sailing of the BJP plan would mean “legalising” gerrymandering that could further the north-south divide. Delimitation Bill: I.N.D.I.A. bloc to seek freeze on distribution of seats for 25 years; oppose CEC Gyanesh Kumar's role 'They will use it as a weapon to remain in power permanently': I.N.D.I.A. bloc to oppose Delimitation Bill Sources said leaders like Rahul Gandhi and others referred to how the delimitation commission set up when AB Vajpayee was Prime Minister took almost six years to complete redrawing of existing 543 seats. They wondered how the new commission would finish the job for 816 seats in two years. This means that the ruling BJP has a “blueprint ready” and it is waiting for its execution, sources said quoting leaders as saying. There was also a view that the delimitation under the Election Commission headed by Kumar would help the BJP in ensuring a two-third majority for them for years to come, enabling them to rewrite the Constitution. Sources said leaders felt it was the “last bus to save democracy” in India with leaders like Trinamool Congress’ Abhishek Banerjee and RSP’s NK Premachandran arguing that they should approach the DMK and NCP(SP) to convince them about the “dangers” of the new delimitation bill that provides for a 50% increase in Lok Sabha seats without changing states’ proportion. Congress Rajya Sabha Chief Whip Jairam Ramesh made a presentation in the meeting during which he highlighted that the increase in seats is a “mockery”. He also said SC/ST quota would have a negative impact as the increase in population in the last 15 years would not be considered when Census 2011 is made the base. He also spoke about the impact on federal principles. Congress General Secretary (Organisation) KC Venugopal said they would fight the battle both in Parliament and on streets, highlighting the BJP’s “attempts” to subvert democracy using the Election Commission through Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and delimitation. Addressing a press conference along with other party leaders, Kharge said the Delimitation Bill poses a "very serious threat to democracy" and they would oppose it, as their aim is "not to strengthen democracy, but to concentrate all power in their own hands". Outlining the Opposition's objections, he claimed that the Bill does not take into account the interests of SCs/STs though Article 330 of the Constitution maintains that seats should be reserved for Dalits and tribals in proportion to their population. "When a new Census is about to take place, why is it not waiting for those figures? Under the latest Census, their seats should be determined in proportion to the SC/ST population. Why is the government avoiding giving SC/STs their rightful share according to their population," he said. He also said the Election Commission that is facing "serious questions" over the removal of around 13.3 crore names from electoral rolls is being entrusted with the responsibility of delimitation, which they "cannot accept". "There are already serious questions about the impartiality of the CEC. If delimitation takes place under his supervision, what guarantee is there of its impartiality?" he said. DH had on November 20 reported that the I.N.D.I.A bloc would oppose any role for Kumar in the delimitation process. Kharge also referred to delimitation carried out in Assam and Jammu and Kashmir, alleging that one can see the political consequences of how constituency boundaries were changed on the basis of geography and population, and how the character of general and reserved seats was altered. "We fear that the BJP wants to serve its political interests by carrying out the same kind of delimitation across the entire country," he said.

articles.title: DH Deciphers | What the new delimitation bill proposes and how it will change Lok Sabha seats
articles.summary: Parliament will meet on Monday to take up the Constitution (132 nd Amendment) Bill, 2026 and related legislation that would usher in a new delimitation regime in the country. Shemin Joy explains the contours of delimitation and what is in the bill, approved by the Union Cabinet. What is delimitation? Delimitation is the exercise of determining allocation of seats to each state based on population and fixing the boundaries of constituencies. Article 81 and Article 170 provide for the maximum number of seats in the Lok Sabha and Assemblies respectively can have. Articles 82 and 170 stipulate that on completion of every census, the allocation of seats will be re-adjusted according to population. Delimitation was done in the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s following the corresponding census. Lok Sabha numbers increased from 489 to 543 during this period. However, in 1976, Parliament froze the readjustment of seats on the basis of population owing to the differences in population growth in the south and north. The argument was that population control methods were more successful in the south and a delimitation based on population would be detrimental to the representation of southern states. It was initially frozen for 25 years and later extended for another 25 years in 2001. What is the present position on delimitation? After the amendments in Article 81 and 82, the number of Lok Sabha seats were fixed at 543. The boundaries were redrawn once in 2008 on the basis of the 2001 census though the total number of seats remained unchanged. This arrangement was to end in 2026 as the Constitution maintained that a new delimitation should be initiated on the basis of a Census conducted after 2026. Had this been played out, the number of seats in southern states would have decreased while states like Uttar Pradesh would have seen an increase in numbers. BRS to support Delimitation bill, proposed 50% increase in seats addresses our key concern: KT Rama Rao How is delimitation rolled out? The Constitution empowers the government to set up a Delimitation Commission, headed by a serving or former Supreme Court judge. The Chief Election Commissioner or an Election Commissioner recommended by him as well as State Election Commissioners in respective states will be members of the Commission. The Election Commission will also double up as Delimitation Commission. How does the delimitation exercise designed in the Constitution (132 nd Amendment) Bill, 2026 differ from earlier ones? The existing framework allows Lok Sabha to have a maximum of 550 seats and Assemblies 500. This has been increased to 850 and 650 respectively. The bill now allows a 50% increase in the existing 543 seats while maintaining the seat proportion of states as defined by the 1971 Census. This would mean that the increase in number of seats is not linked to population but the proportion of seats in each state has been fixed on the basis of 1971. For example, Lok Sabha seats in Karnataka will increase from 28 to 42, while ensuring that the existing 5.15% proportion is maintained in the new system also. The redrawing of boundaries of constituencies will be done on the basis of the 2011 Census. Also, a 33% quota for women will be introduced along with the increase. The 50% rise in total seats would mean the number of Lok Sabha seats will increase from 543 to 816. Of the 816 total seats, 272 will be earmarked for women. The proportion of seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes will remain unchanged. 'They will use it as a weapon to remain in power permanently': I.N.D.I.A. bloc to oppose Delimitation Bill After the April set back, will the government be able to pass the bill? In April, the Narendra Modi government’s attempt to push the bills came to a naught after a united Opposition ensured that it did not get the Constitutionally required two-third majority for amending the Constitution. The bill had linked the delimitation to the 2011 census and did not include the provision for a 50% flat increase in seats though Home Minister Amit Shah made oral assurances in Lok Sabha. Following this, the government reached out to parties like DMK and NCP-(SP) with a new formula by including a 50% rise in the text of the bill as well as ensuring that the existing proportion is not disturbed. At present, the ruling NDA has 321 MPs and expects the support of DMK (22), NCP-SP (8) and YSR Congress (4), taking its tally to 355, which is five less than the required 360 votes to get the bill passed. The government expects to get support from some more MPs. In April, the government could get only 298 votes while the Opposition had 230, which is all set to dwindle.

articles.title: Delhi High Court restrains Old Monk makers from bottling 'iQ' gin packaging similar to 'Greater Than' gin
articles.summary: New Delhi: The Delhi High Court has restrained Old Monk makers from bottling its 'iQ' gin in a get-up which is deceptively similar to that of 'Greater Than' gin. The high court clarified that Mohan Meakin Limited, which manufactures Old Monk and iQ gin, is not restrained from using the mark 'IQ' or its 'iQ' device for gin or for any other goods and added that the company was at liberty to sell its gin in a different get-up. Justice Purushaindra Kumar Kaurav said plaintiff Nao Spirits And Beverages Private Limited, which manufactures and sells 'Greater Than' gin, has no monopoly over the colours black and white, and the defendant (Mohan Meakin) is free to use them in a manner which does not result in a get-up deceptively similar to that of the plaintiff. "The new get-up must differ not merely in the shape of the bottle, but also in its dress, that is, the size and placement of the label, the colour arrangement, the placement of the device, and the typography and arrangement of the words on the label, so that the overall get-up, seen as a whole, is not deceptively similar to that of the plaintiff," the high court said while passing an interim order on November 26. Old Monk drops ‘7 years blend’ claim as revised label reaches Bombay HC; it 'can't be sold as rum', FSSAI tells court According to the plaintiff, Greater Than is its flagship product, and it is a London Dry Gin introduced in India in 2016 and one of the first homegrown craft gins in the Indian market. The plaintiff's counsel said it is a case of passing off of the overall get-up of the plaintiff's gin, that is, the shape of its bottle together with its trade dress. He contended that the defendant has copied the bottle along with the black-and-white scheme, the black cap, the placement of a large black angular device at the top centre of the label and the arrangement of 'LONDON DRY' in small letters over 'GIN' in large letters. The defendant, which has been in the liquor trade for over 160 years, sells brands including Old Monk, Big Ben London gin and Jamun gin. It submitted that it has been using the mark 'IQ' for beer since 1996 and launched gin under the impugned 'iQ' label in August 2023. Its counsel submitted that there is no similarity between 'Greater Than' and 'iQ', and the plaintiff has no registration for its label or its bottle. The counsel submitted that the bottle is an ordinary, generic and functional bottle and identical bottles are sold across the world and offered as stock designs by glass makers. In India, Haku vodka and Indri whisky use similar bottles, he added. The court, however, said it was prima facie satisfied that the use of the impugned get-up by the defendant was likely to cause confusion and deception, including confusion as to affiliation, sponsorship or connection, among ordinary consumers as well as among the plaintiff's loyal consumers and the trade. It said the plaintiff has made out a strong prima facie case of passing off in respect of the overall get-up of the defendant's iQ gin. "The balance of convenience is also in favour of the plaintiff. The plaintiff has used its get-up since 2016 and has built its goodwill on it. "The defendant entered the market with the impugned get-up only in August 2023. The defendant is an established company with several brands and a large turnover. "The order proposed does not stop it from selling gin, or from using the mark 'IQ'; it only requires the defendant to sell its gin in a get-up of its own," the court said. It further said that the inconvenience to the defendant of changing the dress of one product is far less than the harm to the plaintiff if the impugned get-up continues in the market during the pendency of the suit. McDowell's, Antiquity Blue, Old Monk banned in India? Know why FSSAI flagged these liquor brands for violations Public interest also lies in ensuring that consumers are not misled about the source of what they buy, the high court said. It directed that till the disposal of the suit, the defendant is restrained from manufacturing, bottling, selling, offering for sale, distributing, displaying or otherwise dealing in gin in the existing get-up. Considering that the products are liquor, sold through licensed channels under state excise regimes, the court said the defendant should file an affidavit within two weeks disclosing its stock of iQ gin in the existing get-up, at its premises, with its distributors or in transit. The court asked the defendant not to manufacture or bottle any fresh stock of gin in this get-up and not to place any fresh order for these bottles. It granted one month's time to the defendant to exhaust the existing stock after which the company should ensure that the product is removed from the shelves of the retail/wholesale outlets supplied by it or through its distributors. articles.title: Let AI do the 'boring' work, decisions must belong to judges: Ex-CJI Chandrachud
articles.summary: New Delhi: Former Chief Justice of India D Y Chandrachud on Saturday said artificial intelligence can help courts with dull and routine tasks but stressed that the decision and the reasons for it must remain the responsibility of the judge. Speaking at an event on ‘AI for all: AI governance and trust, the case for judicial access and an empowered India’, he said a human being must decide and sign every judgment. “Look at what these (AI) tools have in common: transcription, translation, listing, scrutiny of defects. It is dull work, and it is where a court loses most of its time. The tragedy of the Indian judicial system is that judges spend their time doing work which should least occupy their time, dull and routine work when their work should be really concentrated on real-time decision making,” Chandrachud said. “I have come to think that the best use of AI in a court is the boring one. The trouble begins when the technology is asked to do something more interesting,” he added. Referring to instances of AI-generated fake legal citations, Chandrachud cited two Supreme Court cases involving fabricated references to judicial precedents. In one case, a trial court in Andhra Pradesh relied on four Supreme Court judgments that did not exist. The apex court later held that a decision based on non-existent judgments was not merely an error but misconduct, he said. In another case, a tribunal’s orders cited genuine Supreme Court judgments but included fabricated passages attributed to them, he added. “A citation of a law report that does not exist can be caught in 30 seconds. A real judgment with an invented paragraph will pass every casual check,” Chandrachud said. “Every citation and every translation produced by a machine must be checked by a human being, and a record must be kept of each use,” he added. The former CJI said the Supreme Court’s AI Committee had published draft regulations on the use of artificial intelligence in courts on June 3 this year. He said the proposed regulations were intended to apply from the Supreme Court to trial courts and tribunals, and were based on the principles of human primacy, transparency, accountability, data protection and judicial independence. Chandrachud said the draft regulations permitted the use of AI for case management, transcription, translation and research, but prohibited its use for assessing a person’s risk for bail or determining the credibility of a witness. “They (the draft regulations) bar opaque systems wherever rights or liberty are at stake. They propose a register of every AI tool a court uses and a database of incidents when something goes wrong. Parties who use AI in their submissions would have to say so,” he said. Suggesting three areas that required attention before the regulations are finalised, Chandrachud called for a mechanism allowing litigants to challenge AI-related errors, including mistranslations, training for district judges and independent audits. He also outlined five tests for the use of AI in courts. “The first test is that a human being decides and signs. A judgment is an exercise of public power by a person who has taken an oath, gives reasons for the decision, and remains accountable through the appellate processes,” he said. “A language model that has taken no oath; it cannot be asked to explain itself in a higher form, and it does not lose sleep over an innocent man in custody. Let it find the papers, translate them, and summarise them. The decision and the reasons for it must belong to the judge,” Chandrachud said. Ex CJI Chandrachud-led mediation fails, Kapur family trust dispute heads for court battle The second test, he said, was that a person’s liberty must never be determined by a probability score. “A bail decision requires the court to consider the individual before it, the allegations, the material on the record, and the circumstances of the case. A risk score may provide certain information based on patterns but it cannot replace an individual assessment. Any use of such technology must therefore remain consistent with the constitutional protection of liberty under Article 21,” he said. The third test was that litigants must be informed when AI has been used in their cases. “If a tool was used to translate my evidence or summarise my appeal, I should be able to find that out, and I should be able to say that it got something wrong, terribly wrong. That is why I ask you to remember that our translated judgments are vetted by human beings,” he said. “A translation that nobody has checked is a rumour about a judgment,” he added. The fourth test, he said, was that technology should reach people at the end of the queue. “The strongest case for AI in our courts is the judgment that reaches a litigant in Marathi or Assamese on the day it is delivered, and the next date of hearing that can be asked for by a voice on a basic phone,” Chandrachud said. The fifth test was data security. He advocated a sovereign database and an India-built AI model. “None of these tests is hostile to technology. Each one describes what a good judge already does,” he said. Chandrachud also underlined the need for technological assistance in the justice system, given the large backlog of cases. Citing a statement made by the Law Minister in the Rajya Sabha in July this year, he said about 5.64 crore cases were pending across courts in the country. India had roughly 15 judges per 10 lakh people, against the Law Commission’s recommendation of 50 judges per 10 lakh people made in 1987, while a district court judge handled about 2,200 cases on average, he said. The former CJI also referred to legal aid spending of Rs 6.46 per person annually, according to the India Justice Report. “That will not buy a cup of tea in most places,” he said. Listing technology initiatives already under way, Chandrachud mentioned the use of AI for transcribing court arguments and the Supreme Court’s translation tool Suvas, which has translated judgments into 18 Indian languages. He also referred to the use of speech-to-text technology to record witness depositions in all trial courts in Kerala since November 1, 2025. A tool being tested in collaboration with IIT Madras would help identify defects in fresh court filings, he said. Chandrachud also had a word of advice for the legal profession, saying lawyers must read judgments in full before citing them. He said, citing the Bar Council of India’s position, that advocates could not blame technology for errors in their submissions.

articles.title: This team needs direction, I am happy to drive it forward: Rohit Sharma
articles.summary: After being reappointed as the Mumbai Indians captain, Rohit Sharma said the team needed a direction and that he was happy to drive it forward. Kieron Pollard named as Mumbai Indians head coach ahead of IPL 2027 "My honest thought initially was, I'm not prepared for this right now. I had to go back and think about it because a lot had happened," Rohit said in a video posted by MI, referring to his conversation with team owner Akash Ambani following the ninth place finish in IPL 2026. "I'm not saying that this team needs me as a leader. But this team needs a direction right now. And whatever that direction is, if it is me, I'm more than happy to drive this team forward. I went home and thought about it. I understood what I can do and what I can't do. Whether I can captain this team again or not. And all of that. "But then, after thinking about so many things, I realised that this is the team that you built. For 10 years, you captained this team. I think it's time you try and accept that challenge again." Rohit has been appointed captain for next season till now. The World Cup winning skipper said the players need to enjoy their time on the field. "Disappointment was not about qualification. Disappointment was that we were not playing well. The responsibilities that people had were not being fulfilled properly. Which again, you know, is a very natural thing to happen when you're losing, the momentum is not with you. "The other teams are playing well. They're trying and capitalising more on you, putting more pressure on you. And we were not responding to that pressure. And that includes everyone. Not just one or two players. The entire MI was failing," he said. IPL 2027: 'Hitman' is back! Rohit Sharma returns as Mumbai Indians skipper He is looking forward to working alongside longtime teammate Kieron Pollard, who has been promoted to the head coach's position. "Polly has been an MI legend, there is no doubt about it. For so many years he has put his hand up and bailed the team out of the worst possible situations. He has been in a coaching role for a few years now, as a batting coach, so he is quite aware of what is happening with the team and understands the value of this team, its culture and what it means to play for MI," said Rohit. "When I was captaining, he was the vice-captain. I used to go to him, so we have talked about such things many times. What I will be looking forward to is not looking at him like a head coach or someone in a particular position, but like a friend," he said. Next year could be Rohit's last in international cricket and a mega auction follows the 2027 IPL. The 39-year-old is not looking too far ahead. "It's a very exciting year, no doubt about it. But look, I don't want to think way too far ahead. What comes in front of me, I want to treat that first and then keep moving on. That's what I have done in my life."

articles.title: Arundhati Roy, Ashok Vajpeyi among others flag ‘growing assault on constitutional values’
articles.summary: New Delhi: A group of noted writers, artists and cultural practitioners, including poet Ashok Vajpeyi, author Arundhati Roy and dancer Mallika Sarabhai, on Saturday issued a declaration expressing concern over what they described as a “growing assault on constitutional values, democratic institutions and freedom of expression”. The declaration was issued at the National Conclave of Writers, Artists and Cultural Practitioners, a gathering held at Jawahar Bhawan here to “defend our Constitution, democracy, and creative freedom”. It said the participants had come together at a time when India’s core identity as a pluralistic, democratic and culturally diverse society was “under severe pressure”. “We express deep concern about the growing assault on the constitutional values, democratic institutions, and freedoms that have shaped our collective lives and ways of thinking. We see a narrow-minded approach to national and social diversity attempting to transform it into uniformity,” the statement said. The declaration, prepared through more than 500 drafts from 21 states and contributions from creative practitioners working in 12 mediums, said diverse historical traditions, ideas, beliefs and life experiences were “being replaced by a single identity and a single narrative”. Around 100 detained in Bengaluru during protests demanding 'freedom from Freedom Park' The group also expressed concern over the “ever-shrinking space for intellectual discourse, independent thought, scientific temper, and freedom of education”, alleging growing attempts to restrict people’s rights to think, write, read, teach, create and question. “History is being distorted, and the space for critical thinking and independent thought is being curtailed. We believe that freedom of expression and freedom of mind are intertwined. Where there is an atmosphere of fear, censorship, and the imposition of uniform thinking, neither ideas nor democratic life can flourish,” it said. The declaration said the growing imbalance of power was undermining the rights of individuals and communities to determine their own futures. “From Kashmir to Manipur, religious minorities, especially Muslims and Christians, tribal communities, and other historically marginalised peoples are facing a sustained assault on their dignity, identity, memories, and their right to self-determination,” it said. The group also flagged the “shrinking space for creative expression and the growing intolerance towards voices that question authority”, saying writers, artists, filmmakers, musicians, theatre artists, scholars and journalists must be free to “imagine, express their views, question, dissent, and create without fear or coercion”. “A society that seeks to control its artists and intellectuals is, in effect, seeking to control the imagination of its people,” the declaration said, opposing the “normalisation of violence, discrimination, exclusion, and hatred”. The signatories, who also included writers Mridula Garg, N S Madhavan, Khalid Javed, M K Raina, Ganesh Devy, Kazi Neel and Gauhar Raza, pledged to dedicate their creative energies to defending diversity, plurality, intellectual freedom and the constitutional values of liberty, equality, justice and fraternity. “We make it clear that culture cannot be a weapon of power, nor can art be confined within the boundaries of a fixed identity or preconceived ideas. The power of creative energy lies in freedom, curiosity, innovation, dissent, and the courage to imagine beyond the boundaries. Art and culture belong to the people and must remain accountable to the broader human aspirations for dignity, justice, and freedom,” the statement said. The declaration said the group would keep alive memories “that are being erased” and amplify voices “that are being silenced”. “We stand for an India where diverse voices can coexist without fear, where differences are not suppressed but rather respected, where cultural heritage remains a living and constantly evolving tradition and where freedom of expression, thought and imagination are accepted as fundamental pillars of democracy,” it said.

articles.title: Explained | AQI 59 or 1,000? Kashmir’s clean-air image faces a pollution test
articles.summary: Srinagar: For someone stepping out of Bengaluru’s traffic-choked roads or Delhi’s winter smog, Kashmir’s snow-covered mountains, pine forests and alpine lakes promise an escape into cleaner air. But what if the air in this much-sought-after holiday destination is not as pristine as its postcard images suggest? A growing controversy over air-quality readings in Srinagar has raised precisely that question. While private monitoring platforms have reported alarming pollution levels, government stations have recorded considerably lower figures, leaving residents and visitors wondering what they are actually breathing. Sheshnag, Vande Mataram controversies refuse to die down in Jammu & Kashmir On November 20, the private platform AQI.in reported an Air Quality Index (AQI) of 354 for Srinagar, placing it at the top of its live global pollution rankings. The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), however, recorded an AQI of 59 for the city on the same day, categorising the air as satisfactory. The discrepancy widened over the following days. On November 26, non-governmental monitoring platforms reported readings of 1,000 at Shalateng and 698 at Kanipora. The CPCB recorded an AQI of 179 for Srinagar at 12.05 pm that day, while the Jammu and Kashmir Pollution Control Committee (JKPCC) said its readings had generally remained between 109 and 178 during November. The conflicting numbers have triggered a larger debate: Is Srinagar experiencing serious pollution, or are different monitoring systems telling different stories? Why are the readings so different? One reason is that the platforms may not be measuring and calculating air quality in the same way. India has its own National Air Quality Index, introduced in 2015. Private international platforms such as IQAir use the US AQI system, while AQI.in also displays readings using the US-style index. Some private platforms use hourly or near-real-time measurements, whereas India’s official AQI follows prescribed averaging periods. JKPCC Chairman Vasu Yadav has questioned the reliability of private monitoring systems. “Our AQI is analyser-based, while online AQI monitoring stations are sensor-based and can be installed anywhere,” he said. Yadav said the committee followed CPCB-prescribed procedures and that its readings had generally remained below 200 during November. After 2019 reorganisation, Centre moves to restore Jammu & Kashmir's presidential poll representation What do the numbers actually mean? Under India’s classification, AQI readings of 0-50 are good, 51-100 satisfactory, 101-200 moderate, 201-300 poor, 301-400 very poor and 401-500 severe. The Indian National AQI scale ends at 500. Therefore, private-platform readings of 700 or 1,000 cannot be described as official Indian AQI categories. They represent readings calculated under those platforms’ own methods. This distinction is important because AQI is an index, not a direct measurement of the amount of pollution in the air. PM2.5 and PM10 concentrations, measured in micrograms per cubic metre, provide a more direct picture of the particulate pollution people are exposed to. Is Kashmir’s winter air as clean as it looks? The dispute over monitoring does not mean Kashmir is free from pollution. Scientific research has documented a seasonal deterioration in Srinagar’s air quality, particularly during winter. A study published in Scientific Reports in 2018 found that PM2.5 concentrations in Srinagar reached 348 micrograms per cubic metre during its 2013-14 observation period, against the then applicable Indian 24-hour permissible limit of 60 micrograms per cubic metre. Researchers identified domestic coal and other biofuel emissions, cold temperatures and dry weather as important contributors to winter pollution. Air masses carrying dust from Afghanistan and surrounding regions also contributed. The Valley’s mountain-enclosed geography can compound the problem. During temperature inversion, cold air remains trapped close to the ground beneath a warmer layer, restricting the dispersal of pollutants. Household heating, vehicle emissions, road dust and the burning of fallen leaves and agricultural waste add to the pollution burden. Meteorological Department director Mukhtar Ahmad has cautioned against assuming that Kashmir’s air is entirely clean. “It is not that pure, what is being described if someone comes from outside. Due to several reasons, the air quality dips during winters in Srinagar,” he said. Beyond the battlefield: How security agencies are digging into Jammu and Kashmir’s old terror networks What about tourists escaping metros? For visitors from Bengaluru, Delhi and Mumbai, Kashmir is often an escape from urban congestion and polluted air. The expectation of breathing cleaner air amid mountains and forests is an important part of the Valley’s tourism appeal. Government figures for 2025 show that Gulmarg recorded an annual average AQI of 54.75, Pahalgam 64 and Sonamarg 61.83, compared with 94.75 in Srinagar. The three tourist destinations recorded satisfactory air quality. A report submitted to the National Green Tribunal by the Union Environment Ministry on environmental pressures in the Indian Himalayan region also identified gaps in air-quality monitoring at tourist destinations in Kashmir. It said the impact of tourism on air quality could not be clearly established because of inadequate data and recommended regular monitoring at tourist locations. There is no evidence that the current AQI controversy has affected tourist arrivals. But for a region whose economy depends heavily on its natural attractions, the quality of its air is as important as the protection of its lakes, forests and mountains. Is there enough monitoring? The Jammu and Kashmir government’s reply in the Assembly states that three continuous ambient air-quality monitoring stations are operational in the Union Territory, two in Srinagar district and one in Pulwama. Separately, the Pollution Control Committee monitors 45 locations under the National Air Quality Monitoring Programme. The government has proposed four additional sensor-based real-time monitoring stations in Samba, Kathua, Pulwama and Anantnag. The immediate need is to expand monitoring, particularly at popular tourist destinations, and make station-wise PM2.5 and PM10 data publicly accessible. For tourists planning a winter holiday and residents going about their daily lives, the question is no longer just whether Kashmir looks clean. It is whether the air is as clean as the Valley’s tourism brochures promise.

articles.title: Karnataka issues notice to IOC over excess ethanol in E20 petrol
articles.summary: The Karnataka government’s concerns over alleged excess ethanol blending in petrol have escalated, with the state Legal Metrology Department issuing a show-cause notice to an Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) terminal near Bengaluru over discrepancies in the measurement of ethanol and motor gasoline. The notice, dated November 25, flagged “discrepancies in the measurement of ethanol and motor gasoline through mass flow meters” at the IOC terminal in Devanagonthi, the office of Rizwan Arshad, Minister for Food and Civil Supplies, Consumer Affairs and Legal Metrology, said. The notice was served on the deputy general manager in charge of the terminal on Friday. The official has been asked to submit a written explanation within seven days. The development comes days after the Karnataka government wrote to the Union government alleging that public sector oil companies were supplying E20 petrol with ethanol content exceeding the mandated 20%. ‘Excess supply of 14 litres of ethanol’ According to the Minister, an inspection by the Legal Metrology Department found discrepancies in the quantities of ethanol and motor gasoline dispensed through mass flow meters at the terminal. “An examination of the mass flow meters revealed an excess supply of 14 litres of ethanol for every 3,000 litres of petrol. Conversely, it was found that the quantity of motor gasoline supplied was four to six litres short for every 3,000 litres,” he said. The department conducted the inspection using the ‘master proving’ test method. At Bay No. 9, the inspection allegedly found that the meter dispensed 14 litres of ethanol in excess for every 3,000 litres, while the quantity of motor gasoline was short by four to six litres. At another bay, Bay No. 4, the meter allegedly dispensed three litres of ethanol in excess for every 3,000 litres, Arshad said. “These discrepancies exceed the permissible limits prescribed under the applicable Legal Metrology Act and rules. The department noted in its inspection report that this results in inaccuracies in the measured quantity of petroleum products, which could adversely affect the interests of consumers, distributors, and other stakeholders,” the minister added. The Legal Metrology Department has sought an explanation for the discrepancies and details of the corrective measures proposed to ensure the accuracy of the mass flow meters and associated batch control units. It has also asked the terminal to submit records of the most recent calibration and maintenance. The department has directed that the relevant measurement systems not be used for commercial transactions until their accuracy and compliance with legal standards are verified. The notice comes amid the Karnataka government's demands for greater transparency in the sale of E20 petrol. In a letter to Union Petroleum and Natural Gas Minister Hardeep Singh Puri on November 17, Arshad had sought measures including the display of the actual ethanol blend at every fuel station, disclosure of the ethanol percentage on fuel bills, and the availability of lower-ethanol-blend fuel as an option for consumers. He had also called for an independent testing mechanism to verify ethanol content in petrol and the creation of an E20 compensation fund.

articles.title: Madurai witnesses silent protest against SC order in Thiruparankundram row
articles.summary: There were no slogans, speeches, or raised voices. Instead, people sat together in silence, their disappointment with the Supreme Court's latest order in the Thiruparankundram Karthigai Deepam dispute finding expression in a quiet protest in Madurai on Saturday, November 28. Organised by the Madurai Religious Harmony People's Federation and the Muslim Aikkiya Jamaath, the protest brought together people from different religious communities, political backgrounds, and ideological positions. Gathering in front of the World Tamil Sangam, near the Gandhi Museum and the statue of Tamil poet Thiruvalluvar, the protesters said their silence was a message against what they see as an assault on constitutional values, secularism, and religious harmony. The protest comes a day after the Supreme Court, hearing contempt proceedings over the failure to implement its November 20 order permitting the lighting of the Karthigai Deepam at the disputed Deepathoon pillar on Thiruparankundram hill, directed that lamps be lit there on November 28. The court also suspended the temple's Board of Trustees, appointed two former High Court judges as receivers to administer the temple, and directed the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) to take over security arrangements on the hill. Speaking at the protest, Henri Tiphagne, a lawyer based in Madurai and founder and executive director of the human rights organisation People's Watch, said it was a black day for democracy. The Supreme Court’s latest order disappointed many, he said, adding, “I want to reiterate that the country is in sorrow. There are very senior advocates who have called me privately saying how shameful the order of the Supreme Court [on November 27] was.” Tiphagne questioned the proportionality of the directions issued by the Supreme Court in the contempt proceedings, particularly its decision to pull up senior state officials despite the state government's submissions that it had not yet placed its complete status report before the court. He said the counsel representing the district administration had informed the court that only an interim report had been submitted and that a detailed report, including all relevant correspondence, would be filed shortly. The counsel representing the police had also enumerated the steps taken by the administration, he said. “It is unprecedented that without hearing the state, you direct contempt proceedings against 11 senior officials of the state from various departments, despite pleas being made before the court. I don't think people will henceforth continue to trust a judiciary of this sort,” Tiphagne said. He also criticised what he described as the disregard for the constitutional principles of fraternity and non-discrimination. The transfer of security responsibilities to the CRPF and the appointment of judicial receivers to administer the temple, he said, amounted to an extraordinary takeover of state functions. “Today we sit with our brethren who are from the Islamic faith to tell them they are not alone,” he said. “We do it as different organisations from different religions, from different backgrounds, different platforms, different ideological positionings.” He also expressed solidarity with government officials who, he said, had acted according to their conscience and constitutional responsibilities. Tiphagne hoped that the assurance given before the Supreme Court that the dargah would not be disturbed would be honoured, and that Muslims would continue to be able to visit the shrine and practise their religion without obstruction. MD Pandian, convener of the Madurai Religious Harmony People's Federation, said the Supreme Court's November 27 order had shocked Muslims and secular-minded people. “It has become an ego issue. Our silence will send a message, stronger than slogans or speeches,” he said. From the silent protest on November 28 Pandian said the location of the silent demonstration, near the Gandhi Museum and the statue of Thiruvalluvar, was significant. While Gandhi represented non-violence and secularism, Thiruvalluvar represented Tamil identity, he said. The protesters had chosen to gather there to express their opposition to what they feared could damage Madurai's religious harmony. Liyakat Ali, president of the Madurai Muslim Aikkiya Jamaath, said the developments had raised concerns about the future of religious coexistence in the region. “India is a pluralistic country. Tamil Nadu, especially, has never had religious differences of this nature. The courts are now becoming forces that could destroy peace in the country,” he said. Ali said the Muslim community had not anticipated such a harsh order. He described the silent protest as a message to the Union government and maintained that local Hindus had not been responsible for creating tensions around the dispute. “If people here wanted to create problems, they could have done so on the day of the Karthigai Deepam festival itself. These problems are being created by outside forces,” he said. Documentary filmmaker Thavam, who made Thiruparankundram Files , a documentary on the controversy, said the state government could have handled the situation differently by exercising its constitutional and administrative powers to protect law and order and religious harmony. He pointed out that the dispute over the Deepathoon was yet to reach a final conclusion in the civil proceedings and questioned the urgency with which the issue was being pursued. Drawing a comparison with the Sabarimala verdict, Thavam said there had been little urgency in implementing other significant court judgements, including those concerning equality, while the Thiruparankundram issue had received immediate attention. He said the dispute now appeared to have become an ego battle between the judiciary and the state government, and expressed concern about what the Supreme Court's latest directions could mean for access to the hill and the dargah. From the silent protest on November 28 The protesters said they wanted to make it clear that the dispute should not be reduced to a Hindu-Muslim confrontation. People from Madurai and Thiruparankundram, they said, had come together despite their differences to defend the region's longstanding religious coexistence. The dispute centres on a stone pillar situated atop the Thiruparankundram hill, about 50 metres from the Hazrat Sultan Sikandar Badusha Dargah. The hill is home to the Arulmigu Subramaniaswamy Temple as well, and has long been a site of religious significance for both Hindus and Muslims. A century-old civil court ruling in 1923 had delineated the respective rights of the temple and the Muslim community over different portions of the hill. The controversy now concerns the Hindu festival of Karthigai Deepam, during which a ceremonial lamp is lit. Traditionally, the lamp has been lit at the Deepa Mandapam near the Uchipillaiyar temple on the hill. However, Hindu groups have been demanding that the lamp also be lit at the disputed stone pillar, arguing that it is a traditional site for the ritual. The Tamil Nadu government and other parties have contested this, with the government arguing that the pillar is a survey stone and that allowing the ritual there could affect the existing status quo and lead to law and order problems. Atop Thiruparankundram is a survey pillar from British-era finds TN archeology report The issue reached the Madras High Court after devotees approached it seeking permission to light the lamp at the pillar. In December 2025, a single judge allowed the ritual , directing the temple administration to make arrangements. A Division Bench subsequently modified the order, permitting a small team authorised by the temple to light the lamp once a year, subject to security and other conditions. The Tamil Nadu government challenged the Division Bench's decision in the Supreme Court. On November 20, 2026, the Supreme Court permitted the lighting of the lamp at the Deepathoon as a one-time arrangement for this year's Karthigai Deepam celebrations. It directed that the ritual be carried out by a team authorised by the temple administration, with the Madurai district collector coordinating the arrangements. The court also clarified that the interim direction did not settle the larger questions concerning customary practices or property rights. However, on November 24, the lamp was lit at the customary spot near the Uchipillaiyar temple and not at the Deepathoon. The Madurai district administration told the Supreme Court that it had made arrangements to implement the order, but the temple's Board of Trustees had not authorised a team to perform the ritual at the disputed pillar. Contempt petitions were subsequently filed alleging deliberate disobedience of the Supreme Court's directions. Why was the lamp not lit at Thiruparankundram’s disputed pillar? What the Collector told SC On November 27, hearing the contempt petitions, the Supreme Court took a strong view of the failure to implement its November 20 order. It directed that the lamp be lit at the Deepathoon on November 28, suspended the temple's Board of Trustees and appointed two former Madras High Court judges as receivers to oversee the temple's administration. It also directed the CRPF to secure the hill, including the temple and the dargah, and issued notices to senior Tamil Nadu government officials seeking explanations over the alleged non-compliance. articles.title: Mired in office of profit row, Bihar minister Ashok Choudhary resigns as Assistant Professor
articles.summary: Patna: Mired in an unsavoury controversy where a Damocles’ sword was hanging over him over his continuation as a minister in the Samrat Choudhary regime in Bihar , the Food and Consumer Protection Minister Ashok Choudhary has tendered his resignation as an Assistant Professor in Pataliputra University. The resignation, after being accepted by the University Syndicate Council in a day or two, will put a lid on the office of profit row which had threatened disqualification of the minister as per the existing relevant laws. Choudhary, a close key aide of former Chief Minister Nitish Kumar , was sworn in as a JD (U) MLC on March 17, 2021, and is slated to continue as a legislator of the Upper House till March 16, 2027. However, he was sworn in as a minister in November 2025, besides being appointed as an Assistant Professor in Patna-based Anugrah Narayan College under Pataliputra University on February 17, 2026. The 58-year-old Choudhary was appointed as an Assistant Professor in the Department of Political Science. However he applied for lien/leave the very next day arguing that he had to serve his duty as a member of the Legislative Council as well as a minister in the Samrat Cabinet. The Opposition cried foul with the former Deputy CM Tejashwi Yadav accusing Choudhary of violating the office of profit law and sought his dismissal from the Cabinet. Bihar: Mother of man killed in 'police encounter' launches hunger strike seeking cops' arrest As the controversy snowballed, the matter was referred to the Chancellor, who is also the Bihar Governor. The Governor’s Secretariat sought legal opinion from the Advocate General of Bihar whether the teaching post constituted an office of profit and whether Choudhary was entitled to leave a day after joining. The Governor’s Principal Secretary Deepak Kumar Singh, meanwhile, opined that Choudhary was not entitled to lien as he was on probation. The senior IAS officer cited Section 68 (2) of the Bihar State Universities Act 1976, which provides special leave to University employees elected to the legislatures. However it did not cover legislators subsequently appointed as University teachers. He also noted that the Assistant Professor’s post constituted the office of profit. In the meantime, even before the Advocate General could submit his legal opinion to the Governor, Choudhary deemed it fit to resign as an Assistant Professor and continue as a minister. “I am being targeted because I am a Dalit,” said Choudhary, who was earlier President of the Bihar Pradesh Congress Committee (BPCC) but shifted his allegiance towards Nitish in 2017 and joined the JD (U). His father late Mahavir Choudhary was a minister in the Congress government in the 80s, while his daughter Shambhavi Choudhary is a Lok Sabha member from Samastipur representing Chirag Paswan’s party – the LJP (R).

articles.title: Parliament's Special Sitting: I.N.D.I.A bloc floor leaders deliberate joint strategy
articles.summary: New Delhi: I.N.D.I.A bloc floor leaders met at Leader of Opposition in the Rajya Sabha Mallikarjun Kharge's residence here on Saturday and deliberated on a joint strategy in view of the government's imminent move to reintroduce a constitutional amendment bill in Parliament, involving delimitation. Besides Congress president Kharge, former party chief Rahul Gandhi, TMC's Abhishek Banerjee, Independent Rajya Sabha MP Kapil Sibal, RJD's Abhay Kumar Singh and Manoj Jha, CPI's P Sandosh Kumar, IUML's ET Mohammed Basheer, RSP's NK Premchandran, among others, participated in the meeting. Congress general secretaries Jairam Ramesh, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and K C Venugopal, among others, also attended the meeting. Parliament Special Session: Kharge convenes meeting of Opposition MPs; Congress issues whip, asks MPs to be present for House proceedings While non-INDIA bloc parties such as the DMK, AAP and BJD were also invited for the meeting, they chose to stay away. "Look, we need to examine this from the perspective of what is going to happen at the national level and what lies ahead. At the national level, if this Bill is passed, the number of Lok Sabha seats could increase to around 850. The first question is whether a House of 850 members can function properly," Sibal told reporters ahead of the meeting. "But the most serious issue is that their objective is not merely women's reservation. We are ready for women's reservation. They can implement it immediately within the existing 543 seats. So that is not their real objective. Their real objective is to remain in power for the next 30-40 years. And for that, what matters most to them is the Delimitation Bill," he said. "They will make appointments to the delimitation body in the same way they appointed Gyanesh Kumar to the Election Commission. In other words, another Gyanesh Kumar will be placed in this position. They will decide the boundaries of constituencies in states such as Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Maharashtra according to their own preferences," he said. This kind of manipulation is called gerrymandering and by carrying out such gerrymandering, they want to remain in power for the next 40 years, Sibal alleged. "And after that, once they secure a two-thirds majority in Parliament, particularly if the strength of the House increases to 850 and they manage to get two-thirds of those seats, they will certainly change the Constitution," he said. A special sitting of Parliament has been convened from November 30. The Lok Sabha has been reconvened on November 30 and the Rajya Sabha on December 2. The sittings will conclude on December 3, subject to exigencies of government business. The Centre is set to introduce a fresh constitutional amendment Bill in the Lok Sabha on Monday to roll out one-third reservation for women by increasing each state and Union territory's seat allocation in the House and the strength of their legislative assemblies by 50 per cent, and freeze the revised allocations and boundaries until 2051. It's official ! DMK to support Delimitation Bill The Constitution (132nd Amendment) Bill, 2026, slated for introduction in the Lok Sabha on Monday, seeks to raise the House's maximum strength to 850, with up to 815 members from states and 35 from Union territories. It also proposes to raise the ceiling on the size of a state Assembly from 500 to 650. The objective of the present Bill is to give immediate effect to one-third reservation for women, including women belonging to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes, in the House of the People and the Legislative Assemblies of the States and the Union territories, through a delimitation exercise, the Bill's Statement of Objects and Reasons says. It says the exercise shall provide for an increase of 50 per cent, in the number of seats in the House of the People and the Legislative Assemblies of the States and Union territories, over and above the number of seats existing immediately before such delimitation . On April 17, the earlier constitutional amendment Bill fell 54 votes short of the required two-thirds majority in Lok Sabha, with 298 MPs voting in favour and 230 against. The government did not proceed with the accompanying bills. The opposition has undergone a churn since then. Twenty Trinamool Congress MPs broke away in June and announced their merger with the NDA-supporting Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI). Disqualification proceedings against them are pending before Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla. The NCP (Sharadchandra Pawar), which has eight MPs and opposed the April Bill, said on Friday that it would back the fresh proposal if it provided for a uniform 50 per cent increase. The DMK, with 22 MPs, has also backed the bill. The BJP is confident of securing the required two-thirds majority, banking on the Trinamool rebels and support from some other parties that opposed the Bill in April. The Lok Sabha has 540 sitting members and three vacancies. If Trinamool MP Kalyan Banerjee's suspension remains in force, 539 members, including the Speaker, can attend the proceedings. The Bill would need 359 votes if all 538 members other than the Speaker vote. Absent members would lower the two-thirds threshold.

The Supreme Court-appointed joint receivers, retired High Court judges Justices S Vaidyanathan and V Parthiban, arrived at the temple premises around midday, escorted by CRPF personnel and formally took over administrative control from the superseded Board of Trustees. Muslims visit Dargah atop Thirupparankundram hill, offer prayers today amid SC's Deepam lighting directive Following their arrival, the receivers initiated consultations with the temple’s hereditary priests to finalise the exact muhurtham for carrying the sacred flame from the Uchipillaiyar Mandapam to light the Deepam at the Deepathoon (stone pillar), with the ritual widely expected around 6 pm. Atop the hill, workers erected temporary platforms and scaffolding around the stone pillar to enable safe access for the priests and officials during the lighting ceremony. A full company of CRPF troops has established a strict security perimeter across the foothill, pathways, and hilltop, enforcing the Supreme Court's mandate of a 50-metre buffer zone around the nearby Hazrat Sultan Sikandar Badusha Auliya Dargah while ensuring unobstructed access for both temple devotees and Muslim pilgrims offering prayers. Anticipation continues to build at the foothill as devotees arrive carrying lamps to participate in the evening ritual, along with senior political leaders and locals closely watching the proceedings. The ceremony will conclude a week of intense legal and administrative developments following the non-lighting of the lamp at the pillar on November 24. Earlier, Justice S Vaidyanathan, former chief justice, High Court of Meghalaya, and Justice V Parthiban, former judge, High Court of Madras, were received by the state government's protocol officers and an official from the Madras High Court. Justice Vaidyanathan, flanked by Justice Parthiban told reporters: "We will read the order copy and function accordingly, we don't want to comment anything on the matter." The apex court on Friday said it was satisfied that there had been a complete failure on the part of the Board of Trustees to administer the Devasthanam. The court suspended the functioning of the Board of Trustees and superseded it for the time being. Workers are also erecting poles to support illumination facilities on the stairs leading to the stone pillar spot to help light the traditional lamp. The preparations for the ceremonial lighting of the Karthigai Deepam at the Deepathoon stone pillar commenced on Saturday with the workers erecting a temporary platform and scaffolding around the Deepathoon atop the Hill to facilitate safe access for the temple priests and receivers when placing and lighting the ceremonial cauldron. The preparations took place under the direct security cover of the newly deployed CRPF personnel, who have cordoned off the required 50-metre buffer zone around the nearby Sikandar Badusha Dargah. articles.title: Around 100 detained in Bengaluru during protests demanding 'freedom from Freedom Park'
articles.summary: Bengaluru: Around 100-120 protesters, demanding the restoration of the right to protest at public spaces across Bengaluru , were detained by the police on Saturday. Demonstrations were organised by members of the Campaign for the Right to Protest, a coalition of civil society organisations, at the Gandhi Statue, Maurya Circle and the Ambedkar statue near Vidhana Soudha. According to details shared by the campaign members, protestors were mainly detained from Maurya Circle. Campaign sets deadline for Karnataka govt to revoke order restricting protests in Bengaluru to Freedom Park The protestors highlighted the "hypocrisy" of the State government, which allows its own ministers to protest at the door of the Karnataka Chief Electoral Officer, but restricts protests by the public to Freedom Park. "We received a notice from the police yesterday regarding the call for protest. Today, when we gathered at Mourya Circle, police asked us to vacate the premises and head to Freedom Park to continue the protest. We tried explaining to them that this was the very reason we were protesting," advocate-activist Vinay Sreenivas told DH . Under the banner ‘Freedom from Freedom Park’, the demonstrations were part of a city-wide mass civil disobedience movement called by the campaign on November 28, after the State government failed to withdraw restrictions confining protests to Freedom Park. The group of protesters planned to march from Mourya Circle to the Ambedkar Statue near Vidhana Soudha. The protesters demanded that the government revoke the Bengaluru City Police Commissioner's 2021 Licensing and Regulation of Protests, Demonstrations and Protest Marches Order, which restricts demonstrations to Freedom Park. They argued that the restriction undermines citizens' constitutional right to freedom of speech and peaceful assembly. The campaign has maintained that protests must be allowed across the city, including near government offices and other public spaces, so citizens can directly draw authorities' and the public's attention to their grievances. AISA students detained in Bengaluru during protest against SIR "Police keep highlighting the high court order. But is the high court above the Constitution of India? Under the Constitution, the right to protest cannot be curtailed," said T Narasimha Murthy. At a roundtable meeting in October, the campaign had given the government November 26, Constitution Day, as the deadline to revoke the restrictions. It had also demanded that cases registered against people for protesting outside Freedom Park be withdrawn. The protest saw participation from All India Central Council of Trade Unions (AICCTU), All India Democratic Women's Association (AIDWA), All India Students' Association (AISA), Revolutionary Youth Association (RYA), Slum Janara Sanghatane, and the My Vote, My Right campaign, among other organisations. "While there are discussions about this matter. This is not something that can be decided after just one meeting. Until a resolution is reached, those protesting outside Freedom Park will be detained," said a senior police officer.

articles.summary: Security has been stepped up at Thiruparankundram hill in Madurai on Saturday, November 28, with personnel of the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) deployed at the hilltop temple and court-appointed receivers arriving to oversee the lighting of the Karthigai Deepam at the disputed Deepathoon pillar. Despite the heightened security, the situation on the hill appeared largely unremarkable on Saturday morning. Devotees continued to visit the Arulmigu Subramaniya Swamy Temple and the nearby Hazrat Sultan Sikandar Badusha Auliya Dargah as usual, with visitors being allowed in after their identity cards were checked. Tamil Nadu Police personnel were stationed around the perimeter of the hill, while CRPF personnel were deployed at the temple. Security arrangements have been intensified ahead of the lighting ceremony ordered by the Supreme Court. By afternoon, the CRPF took over control of most parts of the hill, and security was further tightened. Devotees attempting to go up the hill were later also being stopped. The lamp is expected to be lit between 5 and 6 pm on Saturday. Unremarkable morning despite heightened security In the morning, several devotees visiting the hill appeared unaware of the dispute over where the Karthigai Deepam should be lit. For many, the visit was routine, even as the presence of central forces and heightened security underscored the tensions surrounding the issue. The Supreme Court had directed the CRPF to take over security of the temple and the entire hill, including the Sikandar Badhusha Dargah. It had asked the force to ensure that devotees at both places of worship can perform their religious rituals without obstruction. However, on the ground on Saturday morning, CRPF personnel were seen stationed around the temple, while state police personnel remained deployed along the hill perimeter. The two court-appointed receivers, former Madras High Court judges Justice S Vaidyanathan and Justice V Parthiban, arrived in Madurai on Saturday to oversee the proceedings. Speaking to reporters, Justice Vaidyanathan said they did not wish to comment on the issue at the moment. Justice Parthiban said they would first discuss the matter before making any public statements. Meanwhile, preparations are underway around the Deepathoon, with workers putting up a temporary platform and scaffolding around the stone pillar ahead of the lamp-lighting ceremony. CRPF personnel were also welcomed by some local residents, who showered flowers on them as they arrived. Residents supporting the demand to light the lamp at the Deepathoon described the deployment as the culmination of a long struggle. “People are coming forward to welcome the CRPF personnel by showering flowers on them. This marks the victory of our 100-year-long struggle. They are coming here to provide us with security. The police, who are responsible for ensuring our safety, failed to provide us with protection. However, the Supreme Court has now arranged for the deployment of the CRPF,” a resident said. Among those gathered was Krishnamoorthy, 63, a member of a group of local residents demanding that the lamp be lit at the disputed pillar. He said Hindus and Muslims had lived together in the area and hoped the Supreme Court's latest direction would finally be implemented. He said residents had been deprived of their right to light the lamp at the pillar and expressed hope that the authorities would comply with the Supreme Court's order this time. "I've not seen anything like this in my 70 years of life. But things have been tense in the past two years," Abdul Rahuman, a vendor in the area, told TNM. A section of residents appeared to be going about their routine, with several devotees, both Hindu and Muslim, saying they were unaware of the controversy over the location of the lamp. The Supreme Court's November 27 order directed the receivers to ensure that the Deepam is lit at the Deepathoon on November 28. It also permitted devotees to light lamps at designated places on the hill, subject to security arrangements. The lamp at the Deepathoon must be at least 50 metres away from the Sikandar Badhusha Dargah. The court has also made it clear that devotees visiting the dargah must not be obstructed. The Supreme Court suspended the temple's Board of Trustees after finding a prima facie case of wilful disobedience of its November 20 order. Even though the court had ordered that the Karthigai Deepam be lit at a stone pillar near the Sikkandhar Dargah atop hill, it was lit at the customary location near the Uchipillaiyar Temple on November 24, in keeping with a century-old practice. It appointed the two former judges as joint receivers to take charge of the temple's administration. The court also directed the CRPF to take over security of the temple and the entire hill, while Tamil Nadu Police would secure the surrounding area. Why was the lamp not lit at Thiruparankundram’s disputed pillar? What the Collector told SC The dispute centres on the demand to light the Karthigai Deepam at the Deepathoon, a stone pillar located about 50 metres from the dargah. The lamp has traditionally been lit near the Uchi Pillaiyar Temple on the hill. In 2025, some Hindu groups approached the courts seeking permission to light it at the Deepathoon. The dispute has since led to multiple rounds of litigation and heightened tensions in the area.

articles.summary: Malayalam film director Liju Krishna was acquitted of rape charges by the Ernakulam Additional District Sessions Court on Saturday, November 28. Speaking to the media after the acquittal, Liju Krishna claimed that he was falsely framed in the case and that he had been targeted by a woman filmmaker. Liju Krishna, the director of Padavettu, was arrested on March 6, 2022, after a case was filed against him at the Kakkanad Infopark police station by a woman alleging rape. The complainant, who had helped Liju write parts of his movie’s script, alleged in a Facebook post that Liju raped her in a house rented for the production of the movie. Despite severe health issues and mental trauma, he raped her multiple times, she alleged. She added that Liju threatened her against disclosing the incident to anyone and said “nobody would believe” even if she confided in someone. The complainant added that the assault continued for two years, but there was no Internal Committee that she could approach to file a complaint. “My attempts to communicate this with others working on the movie did not work. He told everyone that it was consensual,” the post added. Days after his arrest, the Kerala Film Directors’ Union (FEFKA) cancelled his membership. “FEFKA is with the survivor. The temporary membership that Lijukrishnan had in the union has been terminated,” the Union said in a statement. The complainant had also demanded that Saregama Productions, which produced Padavettu , remove Liju’s name from the title. She has been under treatment for months, going through trauma following the assault. However, this demand was not met.
