articles.title: Pramila Srinivasan refutes ex-husband & Zoho honcho Sridhar Vembu’s claims
articles.summary: Publicly, former Zoho CEO Sridhar Vembu has maintained the following: that he has not held more than 5% in Zoho, the multi-billion dollar software company he helped found and headed for decades as CEO; that when he moved to India in 2019, he tried to convince his then wife, Pramila Srinivasan, and their son (who is on the autism spectrum) to move to India; and that he had never concealed any community property (joint property) from Pramila. Now, his ex-wife has come out and categorically refuted all these claims in an interview, saying she was shocked when she found this out. “I thought that it would be a simple, consented divorce – because I did not know about this 2011 transaction. He had not mentioned anything to me about it,” Pramila told Forbes US in a new interview. In the 2011 transaction she refers to, she contends that Sridhar transferred his shares in Zoho (ZCPL) to his sister, Radha Vembu, and other family members without her knowledge or consent. In court filings, she had said that Sridhar “decided to make fictitious transfers or ‘sales’ of our most valuable community asset to his family members without their paying any cash or other consideration, and without ever telling me or asking my permission”. Sridhar, today an important figure close to the Sangh and the ruling BJP, moved to India in 2019 and filed for divorce in a court in California in 2021. In October 2020, Sridhar told Pramila over a WhatsApp message that he wanted a divorce, which she says came as a shock to her after 27 years of marriage. “When he had to go to India, I purely thought that he was going to work,” she told Forbes. She also refutes Sridhar’s claim on X that their son, who is on the autism spectrum, “would be better off in rural India”. Rather, she said Sridhar never tried to convince them to move to India, and they both agreed it was best for their son, who is now 26 years old, to remain in the US. Decoding Zoho's Sridhar Vembu: The software czar who became the Sangh's Swadeshi mascot In the contentious divorce proceedings of the couple, who are both 58 years old, a judge in the California court where their divorce is being heard directed Sridhar to post an unprecedented USD 1.7 billion as a bond in January 2025, a development first reported by The News Minute . The court passed the order as the petitioner (Sridhar) “has failed to cooperate with financial discovery and has not been transparent about his finances or financial transactions impacting community assets”. The court also ordered a pause on a significant asset-transfer transaction which Pramila said would transfer a revenue-generating “community asset” in the US to a third party. At the heart of the battle is Sridhar’s claim that he has only ever held a 5% stake in ZCPL, the bootstrapped software products company that’s synonymous with him, which he co-founded along with fellow IIT-Madras alum Tony Thomas and his brothers. This is critical because, according to California’s laws, community assets, which are assets either spouse earns or acquires during their marriage, have to be divided equally in a divorce, unless there is a written agreement stating otherwise. Initially known as Advent Network, the company was renamed Zoho Corp in 2009. Zoho Corporation Pvt Ltd (ZCPL), which was incorporated in India in 2010, reported a profit of Rs 3,190 crore (USD 378 million) on revenue of Rs 13,500 crore (USD 1.6 billion) in FY25, according to business intelligence platform Tracxn. Forbes estimates that Zoho is worth USD 6.8 billion today and that Vembu’s family owns a nearly USD 6 billion stake in the firm. According to current company filings, Radha Vembu, who was never mentioned as a co-founder, is the largest shareholder in ZCPL with a 47.8% stake, followed by their brother, Sekar, who holds 35%. According to court filings mentioned in a 2023 Forbes report, the Vembus’ paternal uncle, Ram Srinivasan, stated in his deposition that Radha had told him that Sridhar had asked her to hold the shares on his behalf. Multiple sources had told TNM that Radha was a low-profile figure who sticks to her role – which was heading Zoho Mail. In January 2025, Sridhar announced he was stepping down as CEO and transitioned to the role of chief scientist at Zoho. “I used my income to support Sridhar so he could quit his job and focus on entrepreneurship. I felt shocked to learn only after he filed for divorce that he claimed to own just 5% of the company he had spent our marriage building and that his siblings somehow owned the majority of the company,” Pramila had told TNM in response to emailed questions earlier. A PhD in electrical and computer engineering from Purdue University, she is the founder and CEO of health tech firm Charm Health and also heads The Brain Foundation, a non-profit she set up which funds research into medical conditions affecting people with autism. Pramila first became aware something was awry with the Zoho shareholding when co-founder and friend Tony Thomas, who lives in the US, asked her to sign some papers from Sridhar a few months after his WhatsApp message seeking a divorce. “Tony brought me the information about how I own 2.5% of the company because Sridhar owns 5%. I then asked him right away, why does Sridhar own 5%? He’s a co-founder, a technology CEO. He still runs the company,” she told Forbes . Thomas, she says, “didn’t tell me everything, but he told me that there are other shareholders and [Sridhar] only has 5%.” This did not add up because she had always understood that Sridhar was the majority shareholder. Instead of signing the papers, she hired a lawyer. Ironically, in 2011, the year in which Sridhar is accused of having transferred his shares in Zoho, Pramila recalls that she had to get his signature for papers when she was about to get a payout for shares she owned in the cloud computing company that she was employed with at the time, following a buyout. In September 2023, the divorce was granted, and a separate trial was set for the division of assets, according to Forbes. Sridhar has not posted the USD 1.7 billion bond the court directed him to. After TNM published the story earlier this year, his lawyer, Christopher Melcher, had posted a response via X saying, among other things, that “The $1.7 billion bond order is invalid, cannot be complied with, and is on appeal.” Sridhar himself disputes Pramila’s claim about the Zoho share transaction, both in court and in a response to Forbes. “I have not hidden any community property and have not engaged in any transactions to defraud my wife,” he said in an email to Forbes . The publication also reported that the long-drawn, contentious divorce has cost Pramila USD 11 million in legal fees - USD 5.75 million of which Sridhar has covered. She lives in a USD 3 million home in Pleasanton, California, the couple purchased in 2011, Forbes said, with Sridhar providing about USD 280,000 a year to her in a combination of spousal support and adult child support. Additionally, Pramila also borrowed USD 2.5 million from her company, Charm Health, to help cover legal costs. In response to an application filed by Pramila, a single judge of the Madras High Court on October 30 this year had partially allowed the recording of evidence of witnesses – including Sridhar and his siblings – and the sharing of certain documents related to ZCPL to be sent to the court in California. The court also appointed a local commissioner to record evidence. On November 19, a division bench of the Madras HC stayed the order and ordered maintenance of status quo. Pramila said that while she was aware her divorce proceedings could take years, she was determined to stay the course because she felt it was bigger than her. “I feel that he did something, like pulled the rug [from] under my foot,” Forbes quotes her as saying. “I feel that this is a bigger problem than just my divorce…I don’t want this to happen to anyone.” Indulekha Aravind is an independent journalist based in Bengaluru.

articles.title: India vs New Zealand: Bahutule rues poor shot selection, backs comeback
articles.summary: Christchurch: Indian batters’ shot selection left a lot to be desired on the second day of the second Test against New Zealand and spin bowling coach Sairaj Bahutule admitted it was a disappointing performance but was confident of the visitors scripting a turnaround in the game. “You can never say that the game has gone out of reach till the last ball is bowled. But yes, definitely a disappointing day. We couldn't build up partnerships,” said Bahutule on Saturday after India were reeling at 116/6 in response to New Zealand’s 356 at the Hagley Oval. India vs New Zealand | Visitors falter after Akash Deep's five-wicket haul “I think all the batters got starts. It’s just that we couldn't convert it into big scores and I think partnerships on wickets like these are very crucial and that's what I think was a little bit where we could've just done better. Shot selection, every batter has his own plan and definitely looking at the pitch they had their plans intact. Some errors happened with the judgment. But overall, it all boils down to partnerships in this situation. Certain players take an aggressive route, it didn't happen. But I think we didn't play to our potential.” Just the batters didn’t make mistakes on the day. India dropped two catches, missed a couple of run-outs and bowlers too struggled to clean up New Zealand, allowing them to get away from 247 for six to 356 all out. A candid Bahutule said India should have bowled better. “To be honest, the first morning we could have bowled tighter lines, which didn't happen because the pitch had a lot of seam movement in terms of creating that doubt in the batter's mind. It’s just that the lines were slightly wider. But as the game progressed, we did bowl really well into the right areas, created those opportunities and personally, I thought we did really well to get those five wickets today. Definitely, we could've been about 30-40 runs short. But I think, you know, we didn't take our catches, whatever chances came our way, we didn't capitalise on that and that hurt us.” Catching has been a concern for the Indians throughout the series and Bahutule blamed it on the conditions. “I'm not shying away from saying that yes, we've dropped catches. But at the same time, behind the scene, work has been done on it. On both catches and direct hits. It's just that we need to just take those catches at the right time. Those are important catches because unfortunately, whichever catch we’ve dropped, the player has scored runs. “So I think it's definitely a lot to do with just making sure that during the game, we put in that effort, what we do during the practice session also. It's not that they put in the work, they put in their efforts. Conditions do matter in terms of breeze and wind factor.”

articles.title: Modi's questions to corporate India expose the gaps in his economic model | Let Me Explain 182 | Pooja Prasanna
articles.summary: For years, Narendra Modi and his government have sold Indians a particular economic promise: make businesses richer, encourage investment, cut corporate taxes, and the benefits will eventually reach everyone else. More jobs, better salaries, higher incomes. That's the promise of trickle-down economics. And last week, the Prime Minister had some rather pointed questions for India's corporate bosses. Where are the jobs? Why haven't salaries gone up? After all the tax cuts and incentives, what exactly have you done for the people who work for you? These are perfectly legitimate questions. But they also raise an uncomfortable political question for Modi himself. If corporate India hasn't delivered on the promise of trickle-down economics, who is accountable? The companies that received the tax breaks? Or the government that designed this economic model, and repeatedly told Indians that the benefits would follow? Across the country, young people are protesting over unemployment, recruitment delays and examination paper leaks. And the PM’s speech now shows he is cognizant of this unrest, he knows it can't be ignored. So, is Modi right about corporate India's greed? And what does his public dressing-down reveal about the economic model of his own government? Let me explain. Corporate India has questions to answer. But so does the government. He reminded the room that his government slashed the base corporate tax rate from 30% to 22%—and for new manufacturing firms, down to 15% . He pointed to GST rate cuts and a liberal tax regime. He even scolded them over product quality, asking why Indian companies reserve their best goods for export while treating 140 crore Indians as a captive market where anything will sell. And then he looked straight at the titans of India Inc. and asked a blunt question: Have you increased the salaries of your employees? Have you hired more people? The Prime Minister has a point. But you cannot spend twelve years telling the country that corporate tax cuts will unleash investments, create jobs, and make growth trickle down—and THEN, when the trickle doesn't reach the worker, turn around and say, well, this is the industry's fault. So, where is Modi right? And where does his argument fall apart? First, let’s give credit where it’s due. Asking what businesses did with public tax breaks is completely fair—and frankly, it is a question all governments should ask corporate India much more often. A tax cut is public money the government chooses not to collect. And there is zero guarantee that a company receiving that windfall will use it to open a factory, buy new machinery, or hire a worker. A company can use the extra cash in any way they want. All those make total financial sense in a boardroom. None of them create jobs. And look at the scale of what corporate India was given. As Congress MP Praveen Chakravarty noted in The Indian Express, corporate India has been handed nearly $100 billion in tax cuts since the September 2019 ordinance. That’s roughly equal to what the Union government has spent on education over that entire period. Add to that the roughly $30 billion set aside under the Make in India push since 2014, which promised to lift manufacturing’s share of GDP to 25 percent. Twelve years later, manufacturing’s share hasn't risen; it has actually shrunk. What did big business do with those $100 billion in tax savings? Corporate retained profits rose to 11.2% of GDP in 2023 from 10.5% before the 2019 corporate tax cut, while private investment remained stuck at 12% of GDP. Or Corporate retained profits rose to 11.2% of GDP in 2023 while private investment remained stuck at 12% of GDP. The government’s own Economic Survey lays this gap bare. Among India’s top 500 listed companies, profits jumped 22.3% in 2023–24—more than doubling their growth from 10.7% the year before — while hiring increased by just 1.5%. Corporate profits were pushed to 4.8% of GDP, a 15-year high. Meanwhile, who ended up paying for this corporate bonanza? The middle class. According to a JM Financial report, personal income tax's share of direct taxes rose from 38% in 2014 to over 53% in 2024, while the corporate tax share fell from nearly 62% to 46.6%. For the first time in India’s recent history, ordinary salaried individuals are paying more direct income tax than the conglomerates they work for. And what happened to the paychecks of those workers? Government PLFS data shows that between 2017-18 and 2023-24, real monthly earnings fell by 6.4% for regular salaried men and 12.5% for women. So, yes, Modi is right to ask what corporate India did with its tax savings. But here is the catch. Why is the Prime Minister acting like a helpless bystander to an economic model his own government designed and ran for twelve years? There are four things he needs to answer for. One, tax cuts cannot substitute for demand. Corporations are not charities. They invest when they believe people will buy what they produce. If a company wants to expand production, it doesn't simply ask how much tax it is paying. It asks whether people are buying its products. Can I sell another thousand cars, another million packets of biscuits, another batch of washing machines? India's population of 140 crore is not the same as 140 crore potential consumers. A household struggling with rent, food inflation, school fees, healthcare, and a loan EMI isn't suddenly going to buy a new refrigerator because a conglomerate got a tax break. And exempting incomes up to Rs 12 lakh does nothing for the bottom 80% of the country who don't earn enough to pay income tax in the first place. As Ujval Nanavati notes in this Newslaundry piece, the Prime Minister seems to have confused incentives with invectives. So yes, tax cuts can make investment cheaper. But they cannot guarantee that investing will be worthwhile. Second, ask why corporate India is terrified to bet big on long-term projects in the first place. Businesses plan in decades, but this government has repeatedly made major economic decisions with little warning. A sudden midnight demonetisation that wipes out a large part of the nation's currency, a four-hour notice for a nationwide lockdown, an aggressive ED filing three times more corporate cases than the previous decade — all of this have made long-term planning difficult. Even the 2019 corporate tax cut wasn't announced in a Budget speech; it was sprung as a shock at a press conference in Goa. And when businesses see one or two favoured conglomerates grow 15 times in market value, triple its share in ports, enter eight new sectors, and corner a massive slice of state bank loans, it’s not difficult to conclude that the game is rigged. Third, look at the glaring hypocrisy of the government’s own record on job creation. In 2014, the BJP promised two crore jobs a year. Instead, according to official Pay Research Unit data, as of August 2026, 8.23 lakh sanctioned regular posts remained vacant across 80 Union government ministries and departments. This includes over 2.41 lakh vacancies in the Defence Ministry and 2.40 lakh in the Railways. Millions of workers have also been pushed into low-productivity agriculture, while secure public-sector jobs have increasingly given way to outsourced contractual employment. And the youth unemployment crisis remains glaring. According to PLFS data, 29% of graduate Gen Z men and 36% of graduate Gen Z women are unemployed. Fourth, if the government wanted jobs in return for tax cuts, why didn't it make them a condition? The 2019 corporate tax cut gave away tens of thousands of crores with zero conditions attached—no mandate to hire, raise wages, or invest in research and development. For years, anyone who pointed out India’s "jobless growth" was dismissed as a pessimist. Now, with youth anger spilling onto the streets over paper leaks and missing jobs, the Prime Minister is trying to shift the blame onto industrialists. If Modi is serious about holding corporate India accountable, the government should publish the scorecard. How much did the 2019 corporate tax cut cost the exchequer? Which sectors pocketed the gains? And how many permanent, well-paid jobs actually followed? Because you cannot take credit for the concessions and outsource responsibility for the results. Indian corporates certainly owe workers more than a promise that profits will eventually trickle down — but the government owes the country more than a sermon to corporate India. Like LME? articles.summary: Congress MP Shashi Tharoor has criticised its former ally, the DMK party, over reports that it may support the BJP-led Union government’s proposed Delimitation Bill, saying the party risks abandoning its longstanding defence of state rights. “I think the DMK has been a very strong voice in the past for the rights of states. In fact, the DMK was in power till this year, and they won't allow the Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas to come to Tamil Nadu because they refused to allow Delhi to teach Hindi in Tamil Nadu. Now, such a party to surrender on the specious grounds that the increase is proportionate without looking at the larger agenda of the BJP behind it is, I think, an abdication of responsibility to the people in whose name they claim to speak,” the Congress MP said. Explaining the Delimitation proposal, he said, "This proportional increase argument is a very specious one. Let's say you're a Managing Director of a company and you are paying yourself Rs 2 lakh and your driver has a salary of 20,000, a proportion of 10 to 1. You announce a 50% increase for everybody. Your salary goes up to Rs 3 lakh; your driver goes up to 30,000. Are you not very much better off? Proportion is still the same, 10 to 1. But you have so much more money, so many more disposable assets, so much more you can do.” He said that the DMK has fallen into the BJP’s trap. Meanwhile, on Saturday, November 28, the DMK passed a resolution in support of the proposed Delimitation Bill in Parliament, as the draft Bill addresses most of the key demands raised by the DMK. It proposes a 50% increase in the number of Lok Sabha seats allocated to every state, delimitation of constituencies based on the latest Census, and a freeze on further delimitation until 2051. The DMK had strongly opposed the previous Constitution Amendment Bill introduced by the Union government in April 2026. The party argued that linking delimitation to population growth would disadvantage states that had invested in family planning and successfully reduced their population growth.

articles.summary: The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) is learnt to have told the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) that it would be in the best interest of southern states, including Tamil Nadu, to support the proposed delimitation Bill in Parliament. The southern party passed a resolution supporting the legislation at a meeting of its MPs chaired by party chief MK Stalin in Chennai on Saturday, November 28. A DMK source told TNM that the 50% uniform increase in the seats of all states, which the draft Bill proposes, has been presented as the lesser of two evils to the southern state. The government needs a two-thirds majority of those present and voting in order to pass the Bill in Lok Sabha. The votes of the 22 DMK MPs will prove crucial. Draft delimitation Bill released: 50% increase in seats, 850-seat Lok Sabha, freeze till 2051 If the Bill does not pass Parliament, the government told the DMK that it will go ahead with population-based delimitation according to the 2027 Census figures. Such delimitation gets legal sanction from the Constitution (84th Amendment) Act of 2002. Recognising the demographic asymmetries that stemmed from differing population growth rates across different states, the 84th amendment had frozen population-based delimitation for a period of 25 years. “Keeping in view the progress of family planning programmes in different parts of the country, the government, as part of the National Population Policy strategy, recently decided to extend the current freeze on undertaking fresh delimitation up to the year 2026 as a motivational measure to enable the state government to pursue the agenda for population stabilisation,” the amendment had said. It allowed for population-based delimitation to be carried out as per the figures of the first Census after 2026. The government is said to have reminded the DMK that passing a law to carry out the exercise would require only a simple majority in Parliament. However, with demographic asymmetries remaining a major concern even in 2026, south Indian states and regional parties have opposed such delimitation. They argue that it will penalise states that effectively implemented family planning and population control measures, which stand the risk of losing their share of seats in the Lok Sabha. On the other hand, states that failed to rein in population growth will be rewarded with a large share of seats. The DMK has vehemently stood against population-based delimitation. Instead, they have demanded that Tamil Nadu’s share of the seats in Lok Sabha, which is currently 7.18%, remain unaffected. A 50% increase in the seat share of all states was conceived as an acceptable alternative. articles.summary: Follow TNM ’ s WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. The Supreme Court on Friday, November 27, refused to entertain a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) seeking action against Italian politician Giacomo Filibeck over his ‘Vote Chor, Gaddi Chhod’ (Vote thief, leave the throne) slogan at the Bharat Summit in Hyderabad, asking the petitioner to approach the Union government instead. The PIL was filed by one Zahid Ali. A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Aparesh Kumar Singh said the petitioner was free to submit a representation seeking regulations on speeches made by foreign nationals on Indian soil. “You are free to make representations. Who is stopping you?” the bench remarked, questioning the need to invoke Article 32 of the Constitution. “You can file a complaint. Why Article 32 petition?” it added. Article 32 of the Indian Constitution guarantees right to constitutional remedies and allows any person whose fundamental rights are violated to seek relief. The PIL sought intervention over Filibeck’s remarks, alleging that he had interfered in India’s domestic political affairs by criticising the government and expressing support for the Opposition. It also sought the removal of his statements from social media. The controversy had earlier triggered a political response from the Telangana BJP. On November 16, state BJP president N Ramchander Rao led a delegation to the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) in Shamshabad and submitted a complaint seeking criminal proceedings against Filibeck and the Bharat Summit organisers. Ramchander alleged that foreign delegates had used the Congress-led Telangana government’s event to interfere in India's internal affairs. He sought an investigation into possible violations of immigration laws and visa conditions. Giacomo Filibeck, secretary-general of Italy’s Party of European Socialists (PES), had raised the slogan targeting Prime Minister Narendra Modi and praised Rahul Gandhi’s campaign for clean and transparent electoral rolls. He also referred to the Opposition’s march to Ramlila Maidan in Delhi, saying citizens must stand up to defend democracy. Ramchander demanded an apology from Rahul Gandhi and Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy for applauding the remarks. He also sought Filibeck’s blacklisting, criminal action against the organisers and a probe into the backgrounds of foreign delegates.
